data.title: Bihar now known for development, not scams and crimes: PM targets Cong-RJD
data.description:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday made a stinging attack on the opposition RJD-Congress alliance in Bihar, asserting that the state, under the NDA's rule, was making news for development and investments "in place of scams and crimes".

Modi addressed a rally in Jafarpatti of Vaishali district, about 50 km from the state capital, where he dedicated to the nation projects worth more than ₹34,000 crore, including a bridge over the Ganga. The bridge has been named 'Nitish Setu'.

The PM, who delivered a relatively short speech, said that he was short on time and had to visit the adjoining Uttar Pradesh.

 

He said the bridge was named after the JD(U) president, who gave up the post of chief minister in April to make way for a BJP-helmed government, "as a mark of respect for his contributions to the state".

"The state has come a long way since the NDA took over. Earlier, only scams and crimes were talked about. Now Bihar makes news for investment proposals and action taken against those who indulge in any type of wrongdoing," he said.

Modi, who was speaking in an area falling under the Hajipur Lok Sabha constituency, represented by Union minister Chirag Paswan, also recalled the contributions of the latter's late father Ram Vilas Paswan, who had represented the parliamentary seat several times.

The PM also trained his guns at the Congress, accusing it of having "misled people with slogans of garibi hatao", drawing a contrast with the NDA government at the Centre over the last 12 years during which "50 crore people have moved out of the clutches of poverty".

data.title: Adani Defence fires four anti-tank missiles in Pokhran Test Range
data.description:
Adani Defence & Aerospace, the Adani Group's flagship defence and aerospace company, successfully demonstrated Bagheera AT1, a vehicle-mounted anti-tank guided missile (ATGM) system, at the Pokhran Field Firing Ranges in Rajasthan.

"The programme validated day and night engagements, a two-missile tandem firing along a single beam against a target representing an armoured vehicle, and an aerial-target engagement at an extended range. It was followed by a static display of the complete system," the company said in a statement.

The No Cost No Commitment (NCNC) demonstration at Pokhran on November 20 was witnessed by senior representatives of the Indian Army, Department of Military Affairs and Ministry of Defence (MoD).

 

"Bagheera AT1 is the outcome of 18 months of design and development, during which Adani Defence customised the missile system for Indian terrain, climate and operational requirements. The result is a complete combat system comprising the missile, automated launcher, day and night sights, mounted on an Adani Defence- designed 4x4 high-mobility armoured vehicle," it said.

The missile is capable of engaging armour at up to 8 km, twice the approximately 4 km range of the land-based anti-tank missile. It rides a laser beam rather than relying on a radio link, making it highly resistant to electronic jamming on a battlefield increasingly shaped by drones and electronic warfare.

The company said two missiles can be fired in quick succession along the same beam at a single target. "The first engages the tank's Active Protection System (APS), while the second is designed to penetrate its defences." Four ready-to-fire missiles on the automated launcher and 8 reloads onboard, providing a total capacity of 12 missiles per vehicle. Also, integrated day television and thermal-imaging sights with automated target tracking. The crew engages from cover and relocates quickly to reduce exposure to enemy fire.

"The system can also engage aerial targets at extended range," the statement said.

India's requirement for modern anti-tank guided missiles remains substantial, with reported gaps in the ATGM inventory underscoring the need for continued modernisation.

The in-service backbone remains second-generation Milan-2T and Konkurs-M, with Spike missiles subsequently inducted to address immediate operational requirements.

India is also progressing with the acquisition of Javelin systems.

"Recent conflicts have underscored the importance of range and mobility in armoured engagements. Bagheera AT1 offers the Army an additional long-range, mobile ground capability alongside man-portable and helicopter-launched missiles," the firm said.

India's defence production reached a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in FY 2025-26. The private sector's share rose to 24 per cent, or about Rs 42,000 crore, from 22 per cent a year earlier, while defence exports hit a record Rs 38,424 crore.

"Bagheera AT1 demonstrates the growing role of India's private sector in developing, integrating and delivering advanced defence systems tailored to the operational requirements of Armed Forces. Adani Defence & Aerospace has undertaken the development, integration and testing of a complete combat system, providing the Armed Forces with a system for evaluation," it added.

Adani Defence & Aerospace, part of the Adani Group, is India's largest integrated private defence and aerospace company, building critical capabilities across land, air and sea.

data.title: Delhi Jal Board plans to monetise land and buildings for revenue generation
data.description:
In an attempt to generate revenue, the Delhi Jal Board plans to monetise its land and buildings to private companies, starting with 'Varunalay', its headquarters situated in Karol Bagh, officials said on Saturday.

Delhi Jal Board (DJB) has around 27 lakh water connections across the city , however the water utility has been reeling under financial losses for the past several years.

"In a recent board meeting the proposal to monetise its properties including land and buildings has been approved. We plan to hire a Department of Economic Affairs-empanelled financial advisor to carry out an assessment and submit a report," an official said.

 

To begin with, the Delhi Jal Board's land and building assets for the Jhandewalan office -- Varunalaya, Haiderpur WTP Residential housing -- Varun Niketan and Jal Vihar situated in Lajpat Nagar, will be monetised.

"Following this we plan to identify other assets that can also be commercialised," an official said.

Located in busy commercial area of Karol Bagh the 'Varunalaya' has six floors, divided into three phases, where the DJB Chief Executive Officer, other Chief Engineers and DJB board members operate. In Lajpat Nagar, the DJB mostly has residential properties for its officers and an old pump house.

Officials added that water tariffs have not been increased since 2018, which is affecting the financial health of the DJB, as loans and interest of the board have surpassed Rs 73,000 crore.

data.title: NGT takes suo motu cognisance of illegal mining near MP's Bajranggarh Fort
data.description:
The National Green Tribunal (NGT) has taken suo motu (on its own) cognisance of alleged illegal mining and frequent blasting in the hills adjoining the historic Bajranggarh Fort in Madhya Pradesh's Guna district and issued notices to five authorities.

The tribunal impleaded the Madhya Pradesh government through the Guna district magistrate, the Member Secretary of the Madhya Pradesh Pollution Control Board, Guna Municipal Council, the Divisional Forest Officer, Guna, and the District Mining Officer, Guna, as respondents. They have been asked to reply ahead of the next hearing on December 23, an official said.

The NGT's Bhopal-based Central Zonal Bench, comprising Chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava and expert member Sudhir Kumar Chaturvedi, registered an original application based on a news report in a Hindi newspaper on November 17 on mining and stone quarrying in the hills near the 16th-17th century Bajranggarh fort.

 

The NGT observed that the matter appeared to involve violations of environmental norms, which could attract provisions of the Environment (Protection) Act, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, and the Environment Impact Assessment Notification.

The bench also referred to the Supreme Court's 2021 judgement in the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai versus Ankita Sinha case, which recognised the NGT's power to take up matters suo motu.

According to the newspaper report, nine mining leases have been allotted in the area over the past decade, though excavation was being carried out at several locations over areas many times larger than those approved under the mining leases.

The report further stated that crusher machines were continuously breaking stones on the hills adjoining the fort, near the Aron-Sironj State Highway, and regular blasting was being carried out to break rocks. These were causing nearby houses and even the fort walls to tremble.

The report also flagged the absence of wire fencing and warning signs around deep mining pits, alleging that inadequate safety measures posed a serious risk of accidents.

It raised questions over the monitoring and oversight of the Mineral Department and the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI).

data.title: Noel Tata's salvo sets stage for stormy Tata Sons board meet next week
data.description:
Tata Trusts Chairman and Tata Sons nominee director Noel Tata has renewed his demand for the audio and video recordings of a contentious board meeting of the group holding company held on September 17, 2026, while questioning the validity of N Chandrasekaran's reappointment and flagging alleged conflict-of-interest concerns involving nominee director Venu Srinivasan.
 
In a fresh letter dated November 20, addressed to Suprakash Mukhopadhyay, company secretary and group corporate secretary at Tata Sons, and copied to all directors, including chairman Chandrasekaran, Noel expressed disappointment with the company's response to his earlier requests for the recordings and other documents.
 
The latest communication comes days before the next Tata Sons board meeting, scheduled for November 26, at which the minutes of the September 17 meeting are expected to come up for confirmation.
 
 
"Of the requests made in my letter of 26 October 2026, you have furnished two documents: a notice of interest dated 10 April 2025 and the agenda and unsigned minutes of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee. The remaining requests are either refused or passed over," Noel wrote.
 
Noel pointed out that Mukhopadhyay's earlier response had confirmed that an audio and video recording of the September 17 board meeting had been made.
 
The company secretary had said the recording was intended to assist in preparing the draft minutes, that sharing such recordings was not company practice and that they were not required to be retained or shared with anyone, including directors.
 
Noel said this position was unacceptable.
 
"My request is not founded on practice. It is made because the draft minutes are disputed on the most important matter that came before the board that day, and because the recording is the only record of what was said that was not written by anyone," he wrote.
 
He argued that a director was entitled to inspect the company's books and records, whether maintained in physical or electronic form, and that neither the law nor the Articles of Association entitled Tata Sons to withhold the recording of a board meeting attended by the director.
 
"Your statement that the recording is not required to be retained is of serious concern," he wrote.
 
Noel has asked the company to confirm that the complete audio and video recording of the September 17 meeting exists in its original and unedited form, along with its metadata.
 
He has also sought details of where the recording is held, who is responsible for its custody and who has accessed it since September 17. He wants the company to confirm that the recording will be preserved until all questions concerning the meeting have been resolved.
 
If any part of the recording has been deleted, edited or overwritten, Noel has sought details of when the action was taken, by whom and on whose instructions.
 
The letter warned that Tata Sons had been aware since September 18 that the record of the meeting was disputed and that the recording was required.
 
"Any deletion or alteration of it after that date would be the deliberate destruction of evidence, and every person responsible for it would be personally answerable," Noel wrote.
 
He offered to inspect the recording at Bombay House, accompanied by an adviser and in the presence of Mukhopadhyay. He also sought a transcript prepared by an independent stenographer at his expense before November 25.
 
Noel has also questioned whether his dissent at the September 17 meeting was properly recorded. He sought details of when the minutes were entered in the minutes book and who had signed them.
 
He pointed out that the minutes were required to be entered within 30 days of the meeting and said he had still not received the final signed record.
 
Referring to item 9 of the board meeting agenda concerning the proposed reappointment of Chandrasekaran as executive chairman, Noel argued that Chandrasekaran had an interest in the matter and should not participate in settling or signing the minutes relating to it.
 
"Chandrasekaran is interested in that item" and therefore "he cannot properly decide what the minutes of that item should say, or sign them as a true record over my objection," Noel wrote.
 
"Needless to add that Mr. N. Chandrasekaran should take no part in settling or signing the record of item 9," he added.
 
Noel also questioned the process through which the resolution to appoint Chandrasekaran as executive chairman for another five-year term was moved.
 
He alleged that the resolution was introduced without prior notice and on the basis of a recommendation that had not yet been made by the Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC).
 
"The obligation under Section 117 is to file a resolution that has been passed. It does not make valid a resolution that was not," Noel wrote.
 
He also challenged the interpretation of Articles 118 and 121 of the company's Articles of Association.
 
According to Noel, Article 121 requires the affirmative vote of a majority of directors appointed under Article 104B who are present at the meeting.
 
He said there were two such directors and one had voted against the resolution. He disputed the company's reliance on the chairman's casting vote, arguing that Article 121 provides for a casting vote in the event of an equality of votes across the board and does not permit it to override the voting requirement applicable to the two directors appointed under Article 104B.
 
The letter also raised questions over an alleged conflict of interest involving Chandrasekaran's family and Venu Srinivasan, a Tata Sons nominee director and chairman of the TVS Group.
 
Noel said the disclosure available to the Tata Sons board recorded that Chandrasekaran's wife and son were partners in Hanno Infra LLP and directors and members of Hanno One Warehousing Private Limited.
 
However, he alleged that the disclosure did not mention any business dealings with TVS Motor Company.
 
The issue assumes significance amid reported commercial dealings between TVS Motor and Hanno One, an entity linked to Chandrasekaran's family.
 
Noel questioned whether Srinivasan could independently assess Chandrasekaran's performance, recommend his remuneration and vote on his reappointment while a company associated with Srinivasan and his family had a continuing commercial relationship with an entity linked to Chandrasekaran's family.
 
"The question is whether a director who was called upon to assess the performance of the executive chairman, to recommend his remuneration and to vote on his reappointment could do so with independent judgment while the company which he and his family lead was in a continuing commercial relationship with a company owned by the executive chairman's wife and son," Noel wrote.
 
He pointed out that the minutes provided to him showed that Srinivasan had participated in the committee that reviewed Chandrasekaran's performance and recommended his remuneration on June 12, 2026, and subsequently decided on September 3 to ask him to continue as chairman.
 
Noel also cited the Tata Code of Conduct, arguing that it required disclosure where a relationship could, on an objective assessment, raise concerns over a potential conflict of interest.
 
Tata Sons has previously rejected allegations of a conflict of interest involving the two families and maintained that the relevant disclosures had been made. The latest letter seeks further clarity on the matter.
 
The proposed listing of Tata Sons remains another major point of disagreement between Noel and the company's management.
 
In his latest communication, Noel referred to the Reserve Bank of India's November 16 letter asking Tata Sons to comply with the applicable regulatory requirements, including listing.
 
He said the RBI's response followed a letter sent by Tata Sons on October 6, which had not been placed before the board or shown to him before being dispatched.
 
"That letter was not placed before the board or shown to me before it was sent, and I have not seen it," Noel wrote.
 
He has sought a copy of the October 6 communication, details of who approved it and whether it was shown to any director before being sent.
 
Noel also wants to know what Tata Sons communicated to the RBI about the board's September 17 discussions on the listing issue.
 
He said the company was supposed to seek the RBI's guidance on his alternative restructuring proposal, which was aimed at allowing Tata Sons to remain privately held.
 
"Please tell me whether the company placed that proposal before the Reserve Bank and, if it did not, why not," he wrote.
 
In conclusion, Noel has asked Tata Sons not to take any steps towards listing, including appointing advisers or intermediaries, until the board has considered the alternative proposal to retain the company's privately held status.
 
He has sought the circulation of this proposal, along with the agenda for the November 26 board meeting, and wants the company to seek clarification from the RBI on the specific restructuring proposal.
 
The latest letter adds to the differences between Tata Trusts and Tata Sons over the holding company's ownership structure, regulatory obligations and leadership succession.
 
The November 26 board meeting is expected to be an important forum for addressing the disputed minutes and the questions surrounding Chandrasekaran's reappointment and the proposed listing.

data.title: USFDA flags 7 likely violations in check of NATCO Pharma's Hyderabad unit
data.description:
NATCO Pharma Limited on Saturday said it has received seven observations from the US health regulator following an inspection of its manufacturing facility in Kothur, Hyderabad.

The US Food and Drug Administration (USFDA) conducted an inspection of the company's plant during November 12-20, NATCO Pharma said in a regulatory filing.

Upon conclusion of the inspection, the company received seven observations in Form 483, it added.

In USFDA parlance, a Form-483 is issued to a firm's management at the conclusion of an inspection when investigators observe conditions that, in their judgment, may constitute violations of the laws.

"The company believes that the observations are procedural in nature and is confident of addressing these observations comprehensively within stipulated timelines," NATCO Pharma said.

data.title: Karnataka seeks 50 more workdays under VB-G RAM G in view of drought
data.description:
Karnataka Minister Eshwar Khandre on Saturday said the state government has written to the Centre seeking an additional 50 days of work under the VB-G RAM G scheme, which would take the annual employment guarantee to 175 days per job card holder, in view of drought conditions.

The Centre has fixed the guarantee at 125 days a year for each rural job card holder under the scheme.

The state sought the extra days to help farmers and rural labourers affected by deficient rainfall, Khandre said.

The Rural Development and Panchayat Raj minister was speaking after visiting a desilting work site at a check dam within the Adavi Somapur Gram Panchayat limits in Gadag taluk, where he interacted with workers.

 

"Due to drought, rural people are forced to migrate in search of work. To prevent this, continuous employment must be provided under the Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) scheme," he told the workers.

Keeping in view the interests of farmers who are facing difficulties due to deficient rainfall, we have written to the Centre requesting that another 50 days of work be added to the existing 125 days, taking the total to 175 days per job card," he said.

During the interaction, farmers urged the minister to provide an opportunity to take up trench-cum-bund works, which would benefit both farmers and agricultural labourers. Khandre responded positively to the request.

The minister advised workers to enrol under the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY), Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) and Atal Pension Yojana (APY).

Khandre said gram panchayat officials were conducting surveys daily under the state government's Bhoo Guarantee scheme, which aims to provide digital property records, and urged residents to make use of the initiative.

He symbolically handed over digital property documents to two beneficiaries, according to a release from the minister's office.

data.title: Dalmia Cement case: Can a mining lease override tribal land rights?
data.description:
The Supreme Court has set aside the Odisha government's land acquisition for Dalmia Cement's mining expansion. In its November 18 ruling, the top court barred the acquisition of land in three villages of Sundargarh district after finding that the government had failed to obtain the mandatory consent of the Gram Sabhas and the affected families. It also found serious procedural shortcomings in the Social Impact Assessment (SIA).
 
The court clarified how the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, provides safeguards to communities when land is acquired for private industrial and mining projects.

Why did the Supreme Court strike down the land acquisition?

The dispute relates to agricultural land in Kukuda, Bihabandha and Lanjiberna villages of Odisha's Sundargarh district.
 
 
Dalmia Cement (Bharat) Limited already possesses a mining lease valid until February 2040. The company approached the Odisha government, which initiated acquisition proceedings under the 2013 land acquisition Act to obtain additional land for expanding its mining operations.
 
The villagers challenged the acquisition, contending that the government had proceeded with the plan without obtaining the legally required consent from the Gram Sabhas. They also pointed out that the scheduled public hearing for the SIA in April 2021 had not taken place because of Covid-19 restrictions, as revealed through an RTI response.
 
The investigation also found that Ashok Sahoo, a member of the expert group evaluating the SIA report, was associated with Dalmia Cement as its land acquisition adviser. This conflict of interest compromised the independence required under Section 7 of the Act.
 
“These are serious statutory defects, not minor procedural irregularities. Section 7 requires an independent Expert Group. Including a Company linked advisor, as a member of Expert Group compromised its independence and breached this requirement,” said Ramanuj Kumar, partner and co-head - Projects (Energy & Energy Transition) at Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas.
 
Such a conflict provides a separate ground for challenging the appraisal and seeking to set aside the resulting acquisition, even apart from other defects, Kumar added.

Does a mining lease give a company the right to use the land?

Ownership and possession of surface land are two different concepts. The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, governs mining leases but does not transfer ownership rights of the landowners to the company. Nor does it override the independent property rights of people who own or occupy the land.
 
“Yes, the ruling makes this clear. A mining lease under the MMDR Act governs only the relationship between the State and the lessee. It gives the company no rights against landowners who are not party to it,” said Archana Balasubramanian, partner at Agama Law Associates.
 
Surface rights have to be obtained separately, through acquisition or negotiated purchase under the 2013 Act and its safeguards, Balasubramanian added.
 
The court also examined Section 24A of the MMDR Act, which deals with compensation to land occupants for loss or damage caused by mining operations.

Whose consent is required before acquiring land in tribal areas?

The 2013 Act lays down two separate safeguards in this case.
 
First, prior consent from at least 80 per cent of affected families is required when the government acquires land for a private company for a public purpose. This consent must be obtained independently of the SIA study.
 
Second, the law mandates prior consent from the concerned Gram Sabhas, or the appropriate Panchayat or Autonomous District Council, where applicable.
 
“The judgment affirms that Gram Sabha consent in Scheduled Areas is a substantive statutory requirement, not an administrative formality. Where Section 41(3) of the 2013 Act is attracted, prior consent is mandatory,” said Gauhar Mirza, Partner, Saraf & Partners.
 
Neither public purpose nor administrative expediency can substitute for, or override, the statutorily mandated consent of the Gram Sabha, Mirza added.

Can a project proceed if villagers refuse consent?

The ruling makes it clear that the government cannot bypass statutory requirements to proceed with an acquisition by ignoring a refusal of the required consent.
 
Section 41(1) says that land acquisition in Scheduled Areas should be avoided as far as possible. Section 41(2) further states that such acquisition should take place only as a last resort.
 
Section 41(3), however, makes prior Gram Sabha consent mandatory if the government decides to acquire the land.
 
In Dalmia's case, the Gram Sabhas had rejected the government's proposal. Similarly, the 80 per cent consent requirement cannot be fulfilled retrospectively by collecting signatures after the government has examined the proposal.

Can Odisha restart the acquisition process?

Yes, but only by following due process of law.
 
The Odisha government can initiate fresh acquisition proceedings. However, any new proceedings must comply with the requirements laid down in the 2013 Act and the court's findings.
 
This would mean starting afresh by obtaining prior consent and conducting a proper Social Impact Assessment. The government cannot revive the earlier acquisition notifications and treat consent obtained at a later stage as a substitute for prior approval.

What does the ruling mean for mining and industrial projects?

The judgment has implications beyond Dalmia Cement.
 
“The judgment requires companies to treat land acquisition, community consent, and mining approvals as separate compliance requirements,” said Alay Razvi, Managing Partner, Accord Juris.
 
The ruling may lead to closer scrutiny of pending acquisitions in Scheduled Areas, especially where consent records are absent or Gram Sabhas have opposed the project, Razvi added.
 
For businesses, this means that land-related compliance must begin before acquisition proceedings advance. The judgment also strengthens the role of Gram Sabhas in protecting tribal communities against acquisition.

data.title: Article 370 abrogation ended separatism among Kashmiri youth: Amit Shah
data.description:
Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Saturday said that the abrogation of Article 370 in 2019 ended separatist sentiments among Kashmiri youth, and not a single local youth in the Valley is now involved in terrorism after 35 years of violence and unrest.

He was addressing an event at Police Training Centre in Banderdewa near Itanagar in which the President's Police Colour was conferred to Arunachal Pradesh Police.

"After over 35 years of violence, not a single local youth of Kashmir Valley is now involved in terrorism," he said.

Recalling the troubled 90s, he said the situation in Kashmir Valley has undergone a sea change after the abrogation of Article 370.

 

About criticism by opposition parties that the constitutional provision had no connection with terrorism, Shah said developments in the Valley have demonstrated otherwise.

He said the change in the Kashmir Valley was brought about not merely by eliminating terrorists but also by ending the atmosphere of discrimination and alienation among the youth of Kashmir.

Development activities undertaken under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi since 2014 had further strengthened the prospects of lasting peace, he added.

Shah said the transformation in Kashmir was a matter of immense pride for the country and reflected the sacrifices and dedication of security forces and intelligence agencies.

Recalling the turbulent 90s, Shah said terrorism was at its peak and there were doubts about how long the country would be able to hold on to Kashmir.

"Even the chief minister of the state had left for England, while security forces, through their courage and sacrifices, ensured that the Valley remained connected with the rest of the country," he said.

"Today, from this sacred land of Parshuram ji, I want to tell the entire nation with pride that the abrogation of Article 370 has brought an end to the sense of separatism among the youth of Kashmir. This is reflected in the fact that today, not a single Kashmiri youth is involved in terrorism in Kashmir Valley," he said.

Shah said the change in Kashmir was not limited to the elimination of terrorists but also marked a shift in the mindset of the younger generation, with separatist tendencies giving way to hopes of peace and development.

He said development in the Valley had gained momentum under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi since 2014, adding that the coming years held great promise for Kashmir.

The home minister expressed confidence that the transformation in the Valley would pave the way for lasting peace and prosperity, asserting that the experience demonstrated the government's commitment to strengthening national security and promoting development across the country.

data.title: CJI Surya Kant calls for guidelines on AI use, disclosure in legal research
data.description:
Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Saturday urged the Commonwealth Legal Education Association (CLEA) to develop model guidelines on the disclosure of AI assistance in legal research.

Delivering the inaugural address at CLEA 1st Annual International Conference on Legal Education 2026 here, he also suggested that a minimum period of legal aid work be made compulsory for every student to graduate, with additional credits for those who go beyond it.

"I would urge CLEA to take the lead by developing model guidelines on the disclosure of AI assistance in legal research, which law schools and journals across the Commonwealth could adapt to their own needs," he said.

 

Talking about research in the age of AI, he cautioned that no student should be held guilty of misconduct on the word of a machine alone as software that claims to tell whether a given essay was written by a student or by a machine can go wrong for different reasons.

Students must know which uses are permitted and which must be disclosed, among others.

He said tools like AI can help researchers find and organise material, but the answer is not necessarily an accurate one.

However, he said that shortcomings like a fabricated authority looking entirely plausible may occur when using these technological tools.

The answer lies in responsible use, and not in uncritical adoption or blanket prohibition.

The researchers must check every authority against its primary source, disclose any material assistance, and remain answerable for what they publish, he said.

An AI system cannot be credited as an author, precisely because it cannot be held responsible for the work.

He said generative artificial intelligence has unsettled the long-held assumption that an examination sheet or a research paper is evidence of what a student knows.

A tool can now summarise a judgment, suggest arguments, and produce a polished answer within minutes.

"The question, therefore, is no longer whether students will use these tools, but whether the work they submit still reflects their own reasoning, understanding, and appreciation for the law," Justice Surya Kant said.

The simplest response would be to ban such tools altogether, but he is convinced that this would be neither practicable nor wise, he said.

Courts across the Commonwealth have largely chosen to regulate the use of such tools rather than forbid them.

The Supreme Court of Singapore, for instance, permits court users to employ such tools, but holds them fully responsible for everything they file, he said.

He said a ban would only drive this use out of sight, where it can be neither guided nor examined.

"The wiser course is to set clear rules and to teach responsible use, so that technology assists the student's search," he said.

He said many institutions now rely on software that claims to tell whether a given essay was written by a student or by a machine, and it is tempting to treat its verdict as proof of misconduct.

The software used to determine whether an essay was written by the student or not is far from reliable.

He cited a 2023 study which found that seven widely used detectors, though almost flawless with essays written by schoolchildren in the US, wrongly flagged more than three in every five essays by non-native speakers of English as machine generated.

In a Commonwealth where so many students write in English as a second or third language, an honest student could thus be branded a cheat on the strength of a number that no one can explain, and that student cannot meaningfully challenge, he said.

Justice Surya Kant said assessment, too, must evolve, so that written work is supported by an oral explanation, a defence of the authorities relied upon, or an exercise in spotting the errors in a machine-generated answer.

Talking about the importance of legal aid clinics, he said the legal services authority's own scheme points the way, envisaging panel lawyers and para-legal volunteers working alongside students, and clinics that reach out to villages and settlements.

However, he believes that a clinic's work should also not pause with the semester, and students who serve in it during their breaks should receive certificates for the work they actually do, he said.

Legal aid clinics can themselves become centres of continuing learning, where panel advocates, legal services officers and students meet in regular case discussions, he said.

On the question of whether practical learning should remain confined to a separate corner of the curriculum, or whether it should also shape the teaching of core subjects such as Evidence, Criminal Procedure, Family Law and Constitutional Law, he said the latter deserves serious consideration.

With 'uniform citation for the commonwealth' being the topic for a technical session of the conference, he said where a Court has assigned a neutral citation, as the Supreme Court has done since 2023, that citation should serve as its principal identifier.

A shared minimum format, giving the year, the Court, the decision number and the paragraph, would then allow any judgment to be traced and verified across borders, he added.
